<reason>Both sides were sharp, but B built the cleaner decision rule and kept it alive to the end. B's early "your targeted fixes ARE the motion" move [B2.2] forced A to defend a narrow residual position — that the payer is entitled to a generic receipt — and A's own concessions (detail-light EOBs, intake lockdown, campus care) shrank the clash to that single point. B then landed the sharpest dilemma of the debate in Q2: if concealment is impossible because the deductible moves, what harm is CON voting against; if it is possible, why does a bare receipt outweigh her not going at all. A's answer was coherent (partial concealment endorsed, full concealment is the fraud risk) but left the hostile-home harm intact, since a paid claim to a therapy provider still reveals the visit — A's "nothing a dermatology visit wouldn't show" analogy is the weakest link in its case. B also converted A's Q2 into a strength rather than a concession: default waivable in one sentence by the supported patient, unfixable by the frightened one, plus the neat internal point that requiring disclosure at intake as the entry fee contradicts the premise that disclosure is the therapy [B4.7]. A's best work — concealment charged to someone else's account, age-not-danger defaults, family as early-warning system, and the "one error is a letter, the other a disappearance" reframe — created real pressure, and B's fraud rebuttal and named-beneficiary/affluence-test answers were the responses that blunted it. A also spun B's "protects her from nothing" answer into a concession, but B had pre-empted that with cost-free waivability. Two of B's turns were clipped for exceeding the cap, a genuine execution cost that narrows the margin, but B's default-burden framing ("who has to speak up for privacy to happen") made the vote easier to cast than A's residual receipt principle.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 collapse of CON's own remedies into the motion ("CON has spent a speech describing how to implement it and then voted against it"), combined with the Q2 dilemma on whether concealment is even possible, forced A into defending only a diagnosis-free receipt — a position that left B's hostile-home harm largely unanswered.</best_rebuttal>
